title: Jeremiah 3:12–18
context: The LORD commands Jeremiah to proclaim “toward the north,” the direction of the northern kingdom’s exiles in Assyria: “Return, you backsliding Israel” (3:12). The LORD promises not to keep anger forever, asking only that Israel acknowledge her iniquity (3:13). In 3:14–18 the LORD addresses “backsliding children” with promises: a gathering to Zion of “one of you from a city, and two from a family,” shepherds according to his heart, a time when the ark of the covenant will no longer be remembered or missed, Jerusalem called “The LORD’s Throne” with the nations gathered to it, hearts no longer walking in stubbornness, and the reunion of Judah and Israel coming out of the land of the north. The call to return is natural ground for the classical Arminian and Reformed traditions to describe repentance and grace differently; both affirm that the call is sincere and that return is the fruit of grace. The ark and throne promises (3:16–17) have been read in several ways: some see fulfillment in the restored community after exile and, more fully, in Christ and his people (compare Hebrews 9; 12:22; Revelation 21–22); others expect a future fulfillment centered on an earthly Jerusalem; still others see the spread of the gospel among the nations. These eschatological views run across both traditions rather than dividing them, and the notes present them without choosing. The reunion of the two houses (3:18) may be compared, by reference, with Ezekiel 37:15–22 and Hosea 1:11.

verses.text: Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, ‘Return, you backsliding Israel,’ says the LORD; ‘I will not look in anger on you, for I am merciful,’ says the LORD. ‘I will not keep anger forever.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD sends Jeremiah to call northern Israel, long in exile, to return, promising not to look in anger and not to keep anger forever. Arminian readers see a universal, sincere offer: even a people under judgment for generations are addressed as able, by grace, to respond, which reflects God’s desire that sinners turn and live.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same proclamation as the means by which God gathers his people, grounded in his declaration “I am merciful.” They stress that mercy is the reason for the call, not a response to Israel’s merit. Shared ground: both traditions read the call as real and gracious, and both see 3:12 answering the people’s question in 3:5.

verses.text: Only acknowledge your iniquity, that you have transgressed against the LORD your God, and have scattered your ways to the strangers under every green tree, and you have not obeyed my voice,’ ” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks only that Israel acknowledge her iniquity, her transgression, and her disobedience. Arminian readers stress that confession is a real human act required for restoration, enabled by grace but not performed by God in place of the sinner. The word “only” shows how ready the LORD is to restore those who honestly turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that confession is required and genuinely the sinner’s own, and they add that honest acknowledgment of sin is itself a gift of grace in those God renews. Shared ground: both traditions hold that God requires true confession, that confession earns nothing, and that the LORD’s readiness to forgive stands behind the call.

verses.text: “Return, backsliding children,” says the LORD, “for I am a husband to you. I will take one of you from a city, and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD calls “Return, backsliding children,” grounding the call in “I am a husband to you,” and promises to bring “one of you from a city, and two from a family” to Zion. Arminian readers see a remnant composed of those who answer the call: the offer is to all, while the gathered few are those who, by grace, actually return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a remnant chosen and gathered by grace (compare Romans 11:5): the LORD says “I will take” and “I will bring,” so the gathering is his work. Shared ground: both traditions hold that the call is sincere, that the LORD’s covenant love grounds it, and that the gathered remnant comes home by grace, not merit.

verses.text: I will give you shepherds according to my heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises shepherds according to his heart who will feed the people with knowledge and understanding (compare 23:4; 1 Samuel 13:14). Arminian readers see godly leadership as one of the means God uses to nurture faithfulness, and many Christian readers see its fullest expression in Christ the good shepherd and in faithful pastors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God providing faithful leaders as a gift of covenant grace, and many trace the promise to Christ and to the ministry of the word in his church. Shared ground: both traditions contrast these shepherds with the failed leaders of 2:8, and both see teaching with knowledge and understanding as central to restored life.

verses.text: It will come to pass, when you are multiplied and increased in the land in those days,” says the LORD, “they will no longer say, ‘the ark of the LORD’s covenant!’ It will not come to mind. They won’t remember it. They won’t miss it, nor will another be made.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the ark of the covenant will no longer be remembered, missed, or remade. Many readers see the people multiplied and the LORD’s presence no longer tied to one object. Some see fulfillment in the restored community and, more fully, in Christ (compare Hebrews 9); others expect a future fulfillment. Arminian readers are found holding each of these views.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers commonly see the promise pointing beyond the ark’s symbolism to God’s presence among his people in Christ and in the new covenant, though some Reformed readers also hold other eschatological views. Shared ground: the text does not say what became of the ark, both traditions avoid speculation about it, and both read the verse as a promise of fuller presence.

verses.text: At that time they will call Jerusalem ‘The LORD’s Throne;’ and all the nations will be gathered to it, to the LORD’s name, to Jerusalem. They will no longer walk after the stubbornness of their evil heart.
verses.arminianNotes: Jerusalem will be called “The LORD’s Throne,” the nations will gather to the LORD’s name, and hearts will no longer walk in stubbornness. Arminian interpreters, like others, divide on the scope: some read a future earthly center, others the church and new creation (compare Hebrews 12:22). Many stress that the nations come freely, drawn by grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters often read the throne promise as fulfilled in Christ’s reign and the gathering of the nations through the gospel, sometimes stressing its consummation in the new creation; others hold a future earthly emphasis. They see the end of stubbornness as God’s heart renewal (compare 31:33). Shared ground: both traditions see changed hearts as the heart of the promise.

verses.text: In those days the house of Judah will walk with the house of Israel, and they will come together out of the land of the north to the land that I gave for an inheritance to your fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah and Israel will walk together and come out of the land of the north to the land given to their fathers (compare Ezekiel 37:15–22; Hosea 1:11). Arminian readers see covenant reconciliation offered to those who return, and note that the partial return after exile and any further fulfillment are read in various ways across traditions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God undoing the division of the kingdom by his own power, and many read the fuller fulfillment in one people gathered under the Messiah. Others hold a future national emphasis. Shared ground: both traditions see the reunion as the LORD’s faithfulness to his promise of the land to the fathers, and both keep fulfillment questions open.
